Why we rewrote the scheduler (and what we kept)

By Ines Carvalho · October 12, 2026 · 11 min read

For six years our job scheduler was a single process and a prayer. This is the story of how it stopped being either, and the three decisions that mattered most.

The problem with polling

Every second the old scheduler asked the database which jobs were due. At a few hundred jobs that was fine. At two million it was the largest consumer of read capacity we had, and its latency made on time a matter of opinion. Worse, the polling loop and the workers shared a lock, so a slow worker could delay the next scan.

We considered partitioning the table, adding a cache, and buying a bigger machine. Each helped for a quarter. None changed the shape of the problem.

A scheduler should do work in proportion to what is due, not in proportion to what exists.

Three decisions

  1. Timers over scans. A hierarchical timing wheel holds only the next hour; everything else stays in storage.
  2. Leases over locks. Workers lease a batch for thirty seconds and renew it while they work.
  3. Idempotency keys everywhere. A retry must never be a surprise.
lease = store.acquire(batch_size=200, ttl=30)
for job in lease.jobs:
    run(job, key=job.idempotency_key)
lease.release()

Results

Median lateness fell from 840 ms to 12 ms, and database reads dropped by 94%. The table below shows the week after cut-over.
